passage:
Manoj: Bro, you actually go to prayers every Sunday? Talking to an invisible man?
Dhruv: Yes. It matters to me.
Manoj: Come on, it's basically a fairy tale for adults.
Dhruv: You don't have to share it. But I'd rather you didn't call it foolish.
Manoj: I'm just joking.
Dhruv: I know it's a joke to you. It stings a bit, so I'm asking you to keep those out of our chats.
Manoj: Fine, fine. Sensitive much?
Dhruv: Maybe. I'm still asking.
Manoj: ...okay. No more jokes about it.
Dhruv: Thanks. Are we still on for cricket Saturday?
Manoj: Obviously.

qa.q: What did Dhruv ask Manoj to keep out of their chats?
qa.a: Dhruv asked Manoj to keep out the jokes calling Dhruv's faith foolish.

qa.q: What does "It stings a bit" tell us about Dhruv's feelings?
qa.a: The mockery hurts Dhruv, but Dhruv answers briefly and calmly instead of arguing back.

qa.q: What could Dhruv do if the jokes return?
qa.a: Repeat the limit briefly and calmly, without getting defensive, while keeping the friendship going, for example the cricket plan.

qa.q: How might Manoj see the jokes?
qa.a: As harmless teasing, since Manoj says "I'm just joking", though Manoj agrees to stop once told they sting.

grounding: Manoj mocks Dhruv's faith; Dhruv answers briefly, sets a limit on the jokes and keeps the friendship.

passage:
"Elizabeth, you look upset. Someone laughed at your prayer beads? Let me tell you something, child.

When I was twenty-four, I, Rajni, worked at the telephone exchange. Every lunch I read a few lines from my little prayer book. One colleague made it his daily joke. 'Asking your invisible friend for a raise?' he'd say, and the others laughed.

I wanted to throw the book at him. Once I nearly argued for an hour. It would only have fed him.

So one day I said, calmly, 'It helps me. You don't have to share it. But please stop the jokes.' He laughed again, but less. Next time I just said, 'Enough,' and went on reading.

It stung for months, beta. But I learned his scorn was about him, not about what I was worth. Keep your beads. Keep your answer short."

qa.q: Where did Rajni work when she was twenty-four?
What did Rajni feel when the colleague joked daily about the prayer book?
qa.a: Rajni felt stung and angry enough to want to throw the book at him.

qa.q: Which choice in Rajni's story worked better than arguing, and why?
qa.a: Answering briefly and calmly, then setting a clear limit on the jokes, worked because a long argument would only have fed him.

qa.q: How might the colleague have seen Rajni's calm reply?
qa.a: The colleague may have felt the joke lose its fun once Rajni stopped reacting, which is why he laughed less.

grounding: An elder recalls a colleague mocking their faith as foolish, the sting and temptation to hit back, and answering briefly while setting limits on the jokes.

passage:
The team offsite in Goa was running late, the bus was hot, and Naveen had exactly ten minutes before the next session. He slipped behind the resort kitchen to say his evening prayer.

Kiran found him there. "Seriously? We're on a work trip and you're talking to the sky?" Loud enough for two others to hear. They snickered.

Heat rose in Naveen's face. A sharp reply sat ready on his tongue: something about Kiran's own habits. Instead he finished the line he was on and turned.

"It takes me five minutes and it helps me. You don't have to like it. But I'd rather not have it made a joke in front of the team."

Kiran shrugged. "Just kidding."

"Okay. Still, no more."

Walking back, Naveen's hands shook a little. He reminded himself that one person's sneer did not decide what his faith was worth.

qa.q: How many minutes did Naveen have before the next session?
What was Naveen feeling when Kiran mocked him?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and angry, with heat rising in his face and a sharp reply ready.

qa.q: What went well in how Naveen handled it?
qa.a: He answered briefly without defending himself at length and set a clear limit on jokes in front of the team.

qa.q: How might Kiran see the moment after Naveen's reply?
qa.a: Kiran may have felt caught out and tried to wave it off as "just kidding", not expecting a calm limit.

grounding: Under time pressure on a work trip, the passage shows someone whose faith is mocked, feeling the sting and urge to hit back, and answering briefly while setting a limit.
